questions.text: You launched Project X that is based on the pre-investor’s model. Pre-investors denote non-professional or non-institutional investors such as friends, family and strangers who help to fund the project. However, they expect to see a return on their investment. Nonetheless, Project X involves a new social media platform that seeks to generate revenue from user subscriptions. To launch the project, the pre-investors need to invest an accumulative amount of R75 000,00 (year 0). As subscribers and pre-investors join your venture, you expect the initial investment of R75000 to grow, increasing with R15 550,00 annually for four years (years 1-4). In the first year, you expect the new social media platform will generate R110 000,00, increasing annually with R25 000,00. Calculate the net present value (NPV) (assume a discount rate of 10%)

study.title: NPV in simple English
study.section: Performing Financial Analyses → Net Present Value (NPV)
study.simple: NPV tells you what the project is worth today after allowing for the fact that money in the future is worth less than money today. Discount the future benefits and costs first, then compare them.
steps: Find the discount factor for each year using 1 / (1 + rate)^year.
Multiply each future benefit and cost by its discount factor.
Add all discounted benefits and all discounted costs separately.
NPV = total discounted benefits − total discounted costs. Here: R457 950 − R429 997 = R27 953.
study.remember: Positive NPV means the discounted benefits are greater than the discounted costs.

questions.text: Study the cashflow of Project Y in the table below. Calculate the payback period.

study.title: Payback period
study.simple: Payback period asks one simple question: how long does it take to recover the money invested at the start?
steps: Start with the initial investment of R200 000 as a negative balance.
After Year 2: -115 000 + 70 000 = -45 000. The project still has R45 000 to recover.
Year 3 brings R78 000, so the fraction needed is 45 000 / 78 000 ≈ 0.58. Payback ≈ 2.6 years.
study.remember: Use the last full year where the cumulative cash flow is still negative, then add the fraction of the next year needed to reach zero.

study.title: Discounted project costs
study.section: Performing Financial Analyses → NPV and discounting
study.simple: Discounting converts future costs into today's value. First calculate the normal cost for each year, then multiply it by that year's discount factor.
steps: At 10%, use discount factors 1.00; 0.91; 0.83; 0.75; 0.68.
Multiply cost × discount factor for every year.
study.remember: Do not discount Year 0. Year 0 is already in today's money.

study.title: Reading an Activity-on-Arrow network
study.simple: In an AoA network, an activity that has several predecessors cannot start until every predecessor is finished. The latest predecessor controls when the next activity can begin.
steps: Trace the paths that feed into Activity H through E, F and G.

questions.text: A project’s net profit is calculated by:
options: Adding total cash inflows to the initial investment
Deducting total expenses from total income
Adding total expenses to the initial investment
Deducting total cash inflows from total cash outflows
questions.correctAnswer: Deducting total expenses from total income

study.title: Net profit
study.simple: Net profit is simply what is left after all project expenses are removed from all project income.
steps: Add all income or revenue.
Add all expenses or costs.
Net profit = total income − total expenses.
study.remember: Income minus expenses. If expenses are bigger, the result is a loss.

study.title: Weighted scoring model
study.simple: A weighted scoring model lets you compare projects using several criteria. Important criteria get a bigger weight, so they influence the final score more.
steps: Convert each percentage weight to a decimal, for example 28% = 0.28.
For each row, calculate weight × Project 1 score.
Round to the nearest whole number: 66.
study.remember: All weights should add up to 100%.

questions.text:
Project integration management involves the following phases:

developing the project charter.
developing the project management plan.
directing and managing project work.

Monitoring and controlling.
performing integrated change control.
closing the project or phase.
Which phase must be indicated at number 4?

study.title: Project integration processes
study.simple: Integration management is about making all parts of the project work together. The project manager connects planning, work, knowledge, monitoring, change and closing.
steps: 1: Develop the project charter.
2: Develop the project management plan.
3: Direct and manage project work.
4: Manage project knowledge — use what the team already knows and create useful new knowledge.
Then monitor/control work, manage changes and close the project or phase.

study.title: Early and late times
study.section: Critical Path Method → Forward and Backward Pass
study.simple: The forward pass gives the earliest times an activity can happen. The backward pass gives the latest times it can happen without delaying the project.

questions.text: You must choose between embarking on Project Y or Project Z. Return on investment (ROI) is one of the factors you are taking into account to inform your decision. Apply the annualised ROI formula to calculate the ROI of Project Z.

study.title: Annualised ROI
study.simple: Annualised ROI spreads the total ROI across the number of project years so you can compare projects on a yearly basis.
steps: Annualised over 4 years: 12.73% / 4 ≈ 3.18%.
study.remember: Annualised ROI = total ROI divided by the number of years when the assessment uses this simple annualising method.

questions.text: What term is used for the minimum acceptable rate of return on an investment?

study.title: Required rate of return
study.simple: The required rate of return is the minimum return an organisation is willing to accept before it considers an investment worthwhile.
steps: Think of it as the organisation's minimum pass mark for an investment.
study.remember: Required rate of return = minimum acceptable return.

questions.text: A payback period (PP) calculation for a project produces a PP of 2.8 years. Select the option that provides the correct PP formula
options:
PP = the last year with negative cash flow - (CCF at the end of that year / cash flow during the year after that year).
PP = 2 – (-48000 / 59000)

PP = the last year with negative cash flow + (CCF at the end of that year / cash flow during the year after that year).
PP = 2 + (-48000 / 59000)

PP = the last year with negative cash flow - (CCF at the end of that year / cash flow during the year after that year).
PP = 2 - (48000 / 59000)

PP = the last year with negative cash flow - (CCF at the end of that year / cash flow during the year after that year).
PP = 2 - (-48000 / -59000)
questions.correctAnswer:
PP = the last year with negative cash flow - (CCF at the end of that year / cash flow during the year after that year).
PP = 2 – (-48000 / 59000)

study.title: Payback formula
study.simple: When payback happens partway through a year, use the unrecovered balance at the end of the last negative year and divide it by the next year's cash inflow.
steps: Find the last year where cumulative cash flow is still negative.
Take that negative cumulative amount.
PP = last negative year − (negative cumulative cash flow / next year's cash flow).
study.remember: Subtracting a negative fraction effectively adds the fraction of the next year.

questions.text: ______________________ is a dependency in schedule management that is also referred to as hard logic. For example, you cannot test code until after the code is written.

study.title: Mandatory dependency
study.simple: A mandatory dependency is a relationship that must happen in that order because of the nature of the work. It is also called hard logic.
steps: Example: you cannot test software before the software has been written.
study.remember: Mandatory = must happen in that order.

study.title: Activity A: early and late times
study.section: Critical Path Method → Forward and Backward Pass
study.simple: Activity A starts the network, so its earliest start is 0. Because it is on the controlling path in this diagram, its late times are the same as its early times.
steps: ES = 0.
Duration = 1, so EF = 1.
No slack means LS = ES = 0 and LF = EF = 1.
study.remember: Activities on the critical path have zero slack, so early and late times match.

questions.text: Examine the graphic below illustrating an activity on node (AoN) diagram. Activity F's slack is 10 — how is an activity's slack determined?
options: Slack is calculated by subtracting the early finish from the late finish. For Activity F, subtracting its early finish of 7 from its late finish of 17 results in a slack of 10.
Slack is calculated by subtracting the early start from the late start. For Activity F, subtracting the early start of 3 from the late start of 13 results in a slack of 10.
Slack is calculated by adding the early start to the early finish. For Activity F, adding the early start of 3 to the early finish of 7 results in a slack of 10.
All three options provide valid explanations for determining an activity's slack.
questions.correctAnswer: Slack is calculated by subtracting the early finish from the late finish. For Activity F, subtracting its early finish of 7 from its late finish of 17 results in a slack of 10.

image.alt: Activity on Node timing diagram showing early start, early finish, late start, slack and late finish. Tap to enlarge.
image.caption: Tap the diagram to enlarge it.

study.title: How slack is calculated
study.simple: Slack is the amount of time an activity can move without delaying the project finish. You can calculate total slack as LF − EF or as LS − ES.
steps: For Activity F, EF = 7 and LF = 17.
Slack = LF − EF = 17 − 7 = 10.
The same result is LS − ES = 13 − 3 = 10.
study.remember: Both LF − EF and LS − ES give total slack when the network values are consistent.

questions.text:
Examine the graphic below illustrating an Activity on Arrow (AoA) diagram. A node's start time is calculated by adding the preceding node's start time to its duration. In the graphic, the predecessor with the latest start time determines the node's start time. For example, the start time of the node following Activities E, F, and G is 12, derived from the start time and duration of Activity G.

Why is the latest start time, produced by Activity G, indicated as the start time for the node that succeeds Activities E, F, and G?
options: The latest start time produced by Activity G is selected for node E, F, G because the activity cannot start until all its preceding activities finish.
The latest start time is selected for node E, F, G because the activity cannot finish until all its preceding activities start.
The latest start time is selected for node E, F, G because the activity cannot start until all its preceding activities start.
None of the other options explain why the start time of the prededing node and activity that produced the latest start time is indicated
questions.correctAnswer: The latest start time produced by Activity G is selected for node E, F, G because the activity cannot start until all its preceding activities finish.

image.alt: Activity on Arrow diagram showing paths B, C and D followed by E, F and G. Tap to enlarge.
image.caption: Tap the diagram to enlarge it.

study.title: Why the latest predecessor controls a merge
study.simple: When several predecessor activities meet at one point, the next activity must wait until every predecessor is finished. That means the latest finishing predecessor controls the start time.
steps: Path through E reaches the merge earlier.
Path through F also reaches it earlier.
Path through G reaches it at time 12, the latest time.
Therefore the next node uses 12.
study.remember: At a merge: choose the latest predecessor finish, because all predecessors must be complete.

questions.text: What is slack time in project scheduling?
options: The total time that you can delay a task without delaying the project
the total time that you can delay a task to delay the project
the total time that you can delay a project without delaying a task

questions.text: In schedule management, a ______________ on a project is a significant event that typically has no duration.

study.title: Milestones
study.simple: A milestone is a significant project event or checkpoint. It normally has zero duration because it marks that something has happened rather than representing work that takes time.
steps: Examples: requirements approved, testing complete, system goes live.
study.remember: Task = work with duration. Milestone = important point with no duration.

questions.text: Project integration management includes ________________, which involves identifying and managing the points of interaction among the various elements of a project. Its primary tools are communication and relationships.

study.title: Interface management
study.simple: Interface management means finding and managing the places where different parts of the project meet or depend on one another — for example, two teams, systems, suppliers or work streams.
steps: The project manager uses communication and relationships to stop gaps, misunderstandings and hand-off problems between those parts.
study.remember: Interface management is about the connection points between project elements.

questions.text: When does payback usually occur?
options: When the net cumulative benefits minus cost equal one
When the net cumulative benefits equal the net cumulative costs
When the net costs are lower than the cumulative benefits
When the cumulative benefits are double the cumulative costs
questions.correctAnswer: When the net cumulative benefits equal the net cumulative costs

study.title: When payback happens
study.simple: Payback happens at the point where the accumulated benefits have fully caught up with the accumulated costs.
steps: At that exact point: cumulative benefits = cumulative costs.
Equivalently, cumulative benefits − cumulative costs = 0.
study.remember: Payback is the break-even point in time.

You can also use LF − EF = 17 − 6 = 11.

study.title: AoA timing and slack
study.simple: For an AoA question, follow the arrows and node times. The activity's timing comes from the network logic, and slack tells you how much delay is available.
steps: For the assessment's Activity C, the start time shown by the network is 8.
Its finish time is 10.
Slack is 2, meaning it can move by 2 time units without delaying the project.
study.remember: Use the diagram's node times rather than guessing from the activity name alone.

questions.text: A project team must choose whether to launch Project A or Project B. The table below illustrates the respective amount that will be invested for each project, followed by the expected annual revenue. Calculate the net profit for Project B.

study.title: Net profit for Project B
study.simple: Add Project B's revenue and subtract the initial investment.
steps: Initial investment = R300 000.
study.remember: Profit is a rand amount; ROI turns that profit into a percentage of the investment.

questions.text: Examine the graphic below illustrating an activity on node (AoN) diagram. Activity B's late finish is 3 — how is an activity's late finish determined?
options: An activity's late finish is determined by setting it equal to the late start of the succeeding activity. Activity B's late finish is set equal to the late start of Activity G because the late start times of Activities C and F can only begin after Activity G has commenced.

An activity's late finish is determined by setting it equal to the early start of the succeeding activity. Activity B's late finish is set equal to the early start of Activity C because the late start times of Activities C and F can only begin after Activity G has commenced.

An activity's late finish is determined by setting it equal to the early start of the succeeding activity. Activity B's late finish is set equal to the early start of Activity F because the late start times of Activities G and F can only begin after Activity G has commenced.

An activity's late finish is determined by setting it equal to the late start of the succeeding activity. Activity B's late finish is set equal to the late start of Activity G because the late finish times of Activities C and F can only begin after Activity G has commenced.
questions.correctAnswer: An activity's late finish is determined by setting it equal to the late start of the succeeding activity. Activity B's late finish is set equal to the late start of Activity G because the late start times of Activities C and F can only begin after Activity G has commenced.

study.title: Late finish in a backward pass
study.simple: In a backward pass, a predecessor must finish early enough for every successor to start on time. When there are several successors, use the earliest (smallest) late-start value of those successors.
steps: Activity B feeds several following activities.
The earliest successor late start shown is 3.
Therefore B's late finish is 3.
study.remember: Backward pass at a split: use the smallest successor late start.

questions.text: You launched Project X that is based on the pre-investor’s model. Pre-investors denote non-professional or non-institutional investors such as friends, family and strangers who help to fund the project. However, they expect to see a return on their investment. Nonetheless, Project X involves a new social media platform that seeks to generate revenue from user subscriptions. To launch the project, the pre-investors need to invest an accumulative amount of R75 000,00 (year 0). As subscribers and pre-investors join your venture, you expect the initial investment of R75000 to grow, increasing with R15 550,00 annually for four years (years 1-4). In the first year, you expect the new social media platform will generate R110 000,00, increasing annually with R25 000,00. Calculate the annual discount factor based on a discount rate of 8%.

study.title: Discount factor at 8%
study.simple: Use the same discount-factor formula, but with 8% instead of 10%.
steps: Formula: 1 / (1.08)^year.
Rounded to two decimals for Years 0–4: 1.00; 0.93; 0.86; 0.79; 0.74.
study.remember: Higher discount rates make future values shrink faster.

questions.text: Which project selection technique takes into account both the profitability of a project and the timing of cash flow?

study.title: Why NPV considers timing
study.simple: NPV considers both profit and when the cash happens. It discounts future money because R1 today is worth more than R1 received years later.
steps: ROI measures return compared with cost.
Payback measures how quickly the investment is recovered.
NPV converts future inflows and outflows to present value and then finds the net value.
study.remember: If timing of cash flow matters, think NPV.

questions.text:
Fill in the missing word:

An activity or __________ is an element of work normally found on the work breakdown structure (WBS) that has expected duration, cost, and resource requirements.

study.title: Activity / task
study.simple: An activity, often called a task, is a piece of project work. It normally has a duration and needs resources, and it can also have an estimated cost.
steps: Tasks are usually derived from the work packages in the WBS.
study.remember: Task = activity = work that takes time and resources.

questions.text: You launched Project X that is based on the pre-investor’s model. Pre-investors denote non-professional or non-institutional investors such as friends, family and strangers who help to fund the project. However, they expect to see a return on their investment. Nonetheless, Project X involves a new social media platform that seeks to generate revenue from user subscriptions. To launch the project, the pre-investors need to invest an accumulative amount of R75 000,00 (year 0). In the first year, you expect the new social media platform will generate R110 000,00, increasing annually with R25 000,00. Calculate the total discounted project benefits (assume a discount rate of 10%)

study.title: Total discounted benefits
study.simple: After discounting each year's benefit, add the discounted amounts to get the total discounted project benefits.
study.remember: Discounted benefits are also called discounted cash inflows in these financial-analysis questions.

questions.text:
Fill in the missing word:

______________________dependencies, in the context of schedule management, involves relationships between project activities that are generally inside the project team's control. For example, if software is developed by the team, they can create dependencies such as performance unit testing before system testing.

study.title: Internal dependency
study.simple: An internal dependency is a relationship between activities that is generally inside the project team's control.
steps: Example: the team may decide that unit testing must finish before system testing starts.
study.remember: Internal tells you where the dependency comes from; mandatory tells you whether the order is unavoidable.

study.title: Critical path
study.simple: The critical path is the longest-duration path through the network. It controls the earliest possible project finish date. Activities on it normally have zero slack.
steps: Add the durations along each complete path.
That is the controlling path in this network.
study.remember: Critical path means longest path, not shortest path.

questions.text:
Fill in the missing words:

In most financial analysis and net present value (NPV) calculations, the term discounted benefits can be treated as synonymous with the term__________________.
options: None of the terms in the other options can be considered synonymous with the term discounted benefits.

study.title: Discounted benefits = discounted cash inflows
study.simple: In these NPV calculations, a benefit is money coming into the project. That is why discounted benefits can be treated as discounted cash inflows.
steps: Cash inflow = money coming in.
Cash outflow = money going out.
study.remember: Benefits are inflows; costs are outflows.

study.title: Finding activities with slack
study.simple: Activities on the critical path have zero slack. Activities outside the critical path can have positive slack, meaning they have some room to move.
steps: First identify the critical path: A-B-G-J-L.
Those critical-path activities have zero slack.
In the assessment, the activities identified as having slack are C, D, E, F, H and I.
study.remember: A useful shortcut: find the critical path first; then look for flexibility on the other activities.

questions.text: Study the cashflow of Project Z in the table below. Calculate the payback period for Project Z.

study.title: Payback period for Project Z
study.simple: Build the cumulative cash flow until the negative balance becomes positive.
steps: Start: -R275 000.
After Year 1: -205 000; after Year 2: -130 000; after Year 3: -50 000.
Year 4 brings R85 000, so fraction needed = 50 000 / 85 000 ≈ 0.59.
Payback ≈ 3.59 years, rounded to 3.6 years.
study.remember: The payback happens during the first year that changes the cumulative balance from negative to positive.

questions.text: A payback period (PP) calculation for a project results in a PP of 2.8136 years. To convert the payback period into months, the fractional part of the year, 0.8136, is multiplied by 12. Why is the fractional part of the payback year multiplied by 12?
options: This is because a year consists of twelve months.
Because the the current payback rate is 12%
Because the payback period converted into months is 8 months.
Because the payback period converted into days is 12 days.
questions.correctAnswer: This is because a year consists of twelve months.

study.title: Converting part of a year to months
study.simple: The decimal part of a payback period represents a fraction of one year. A year has 12 months, so multiply the fraction by 12.
steps: For 2.8136 years, the whole part is 2 years.
study.remember: Years to months: multiply the fractional year by 12.
